sweep_summary: Western Cham (west2650) is in the catalog as fixed word-final (iambic) stress, deciding source Ueki 2011 with Friberg & Hor 1977 as supporting primary. The sweep list held exactly one stress/prosody-titled item, Ueki 2011, which was already on file from the 2026-09-12 ingest (open ScholarSpace bitstream, clean text layer; I re-opened it at every catalog locator (p.51 sec. 3.7.1, p.118 sec. 6.2.1, pp.135-136 sec. 6.5, p.138, p.163): the quotations are verbatim and the source states the categorical rule ('always occurring on the final syllable'; 'fixed stress on the main, or final, syllable') with acoustic backing, so the item CONFIRMS the catalog coding; nothing supersedes it. The ScholarSpace landing page (handle 10125/101778) was opened on 2026-09-17 and shows the bitstream as openly downloadable. Copies of Ueki 2011 (PDF + text) and Friberg & Hor 1977 (PDF + scanned text) were placed under and listed in there. The directory already contained, from an earlier audit pass, Headley 1991 (Kompong Thom Cham phonology, scanned) and JSEALS 2 (Brunelle 2009); I read Headley's stress passages (final primary stress, secondary stress on the first syllable of trisyllables, p.115), which refine the catalog's secondary_rule wording without changing the coding, and Brunelle 2009 only mentions 'sesquisyllabic words with a final stressed syllable' in passing (p.8). only web lookups of known URLs was possible. Nothing remains to acquire for this language (priority none across the board).

new_statements.quote: [p.163] WC does not have lexical stress; rather, WC word stress is predictable, always occurring on the final syllable. WC disyllabic words fit into the template of the foot with a weak-strong sequence of syllables. Monosyllables are feet by themselves. [pp.135-136] In each case, Syllable 2 – the main syllable – had a significantly greater value compared to that of Syllable 1, or the pre-syllable. Syllable 2 durations were more than twice those of Syllable 1, indicating that WC words are indeed iambic. Pitch excursion and mean syllable intensity values were also significantly greater for main syllables.

new_statements.reading: Fixed word-final stress in all Western Cham words (iambic weak-strong foot for disyllables, monosyllables as feet), stated categorically at the lexical level and backed by the author's own six-speaker acoustic study (duration >2x, plus greater pitch excursion and intensity on the final syllable). This is the same source and the same passages the catalog already relies on; it confirms the 'fixed' final-stress coding (rule_string '01 001', domain WORD). No newer or more authoritative first-hand statement surfaced.
new_statements.check: confirmed by a second reader, with minor differences

sources.note: Fixed, predictable word-final (iambic) stress in every word; disyllables are weak-strong feet, monosyllables are feet by themselves. Acoustic study (ch.6, six speakers): Syllable 2 (main syllable) has >2x the duration (overall ratio 1:2.4), greater pitch excursion and greater mean intensity than Syllable 1 (pre-syllable); pre-syllables are often reduced to a syllabic onset or dropped (433 Syllable-2 tokens realized without Syllable 1). sources.quote: pp.105-106: native word templates mark primary stress (') on the final syllable, e.g. CVCV /pato/ [pa'to:] 'teach', CVCVF /kanon/ [ko'no:n] 'be angry'; polysyllables ''CVCV'CVF with '' = secondary stress on the first syllable, e.g. /panatan/ [''pana'tan] 'animal'. p.115: 'The third syllable receives the main stress while the first receives secondary stress.' (/marasa/ 'maybe', /masatah/ 'from a distance'). Also p.116-area: /a/ in unstressed presyllables reduced.
sources.locator: pp.105-106 (sec. 1 'The Word', syllabic templates with stress marks); p.115 (sec. 3, trisyllables)
sources.note: The one Glottolog 'phonology' ref we did not hold; a different Western Cham dialect (Kompong Thom) from Ueki's Kompong Chhnang/Kompong Cham and Friberg & Hor's Chau Doc; it explicitly marks secondary stress on the initial syllable of trisyllables, which sharpens our srule ('no secondary stress described beyond weak stress').

sources.citation: Brunelle, Marc. 2009. Contact-induced change? Register in three Cham dialects. Journal of the Southeast Asian Linguistics Society 2: 1-22.
sources.quote: Incidental only: 'we tried to find real sesquisyllabic words with a final stressed syllable matching the required monosyllable' -- presupposes word-final stress in Chau Doc and Kompong Chhnang (Western) Cham; the paper is an EGG/acoustic study of register, not stress.
sources.note: Instrumental study including Kompong Chhnang and Chau Doc Western Cham; only presupposes final stress, useful as independent corroboration, not as a deciding source.
